reasons.hook_strength: 'Send a friend the whole note, not a screenshot.' names a specific, everyday habit and its replacement in one line. The first frame shows a friend asking for the desk stretch routine, so the question is honest and the share-and-open payoff answers it.
reasons.clarity_2s: The subject (sharing a note with a friend instead of a screenshot) is readable from the on-screen text and the labelled demo chat in the first 3 seconds. The vo 'Send a friend the whole note.' matches the on-screen text.
reasons.payoff: Beats 2-3 plan a real capture of creating the public link and then opening it logged out in a private window. That is filmable and matches the note_share source (POST /v1/notes/:id/share). The script says to show what is real if the page differs from the plan. The limit beat is stated plainly.
reasons.originality: The history has no prior post on note sharing, but the structure is close to existing drafts. I-02 'Send me that pasta reel?' uses the same friend-request chat trigger, and I-15 and the 03-graveyard/11-zoom-in carousels use the same screenshot-versus-note framing. 'Screenshot vs the real thing' is a familiar format. The payoff here is a different feature (public link), but the structure is not distinct enough to earn a 4. The writer should differentiate it, for example by opening with the receiver's view, a concrete moment where a screenshot fails, or a more distinctive scene than a generic chat.
reasons.brand_fit: The voice is plain and calm, the limit beat is honest, and the CTA is low-pressure. The demo is seeded with no real names.

reasons.hook_strength: 'Signal dropped. Can you still read your note?' names an everyday moment for the stated audience (people reading saved notes while travelling or on weak signal). It opens a real question that slide 4 answers and slides 5-6 qualify. The bridge 'Sometimes' keeps it honest rather than clickbait.
reasons.clarity_2s: The first frame shows a phone with a weak signal bar over a note, and the question names both the problem and the object. The subject is clear in two seconds. The mild drag is that 'it depends on one thing' (slide 1 bridge) sets up a single condition, but the carousel later states three: cached, signed-in device, Skwirl kept open.
reasons.payoff: Slide 4 plans a filmable, supported demonstration on a seeded demo account: note open, connection turned off, cached note still readable, 'show the real result only'. This matches the offline_notes source (cached note fallback when the request fails or returns 5xx). Slides 5-6 state the limits (cached notes only, not the whole library, page must stay open, no cold start, no new-save processing), so the payoff is bounded and earned.
reasons.originality: Nothing in the supplied history (ideas backlog, handbook, posted captions) covers cached or offline reading. The myth-bust structure (belief struck through, then condition, proof, limits) differs from the previous recipe, search and import pieces. It is a new angle, not a lexical variation of an existing piece.
reasons.brand_fit: The voice is plain and calm, and it states limits openly ('Do not count on it...'). There are no guarantees, invented numbers or hype. The CTA is low-pressure ('Try Skwirl. Link in bio.'), and the lavender wordmark close fits the brand.

reasons.hook_strength: "Skwirl Plus tip: fix a note's category by hand." is a label-plus-instruction, not an open question. The draft's own question ("can you fix it yourself?") and the myth-bust format are not carried into frame zero. The audience problem (a note in the wrong category) is implied rather than felt, and a brand-first opener adds no tension. It is understandable but generic.
reasons.clarity_2s: The subject (a note's category, manual fix, Plus) is clear from the on-screen text, and the staged wrong-category note with a visible Plus badge supports it. Slightly diluted by the "tip" framing.
reasons.payoff: The planned two-tap demo (remove the wrong chip, add the right existing one) matches correct_category and is filmable. Beat 3's "category view with the note listed there" is not covered by the cited source (turnOn toggle on the note), so that part is unevidenced. The limit beat is honest about manual and existing categories.
reasons.originality: No history item covers category correction, so the topic is new. The structure is a plain feature tip. It is tagged myth-bust but states no myth to bust, so the format is nominal. Compared with the generic app-tour pieces in history, it is only mildly distinct.
reasons.brand_fit: Plain, useful, non-hype voice, honest manual limit, no guarantees or invented numbers. The repeated "Skwirl Plus" prefix in every unit reads a little like a spec sheet, and the entitlement wording (see issues) is slightly too absolute.

unsupported_claims: Plus only (beats.4.on_screen) and "Skwirl Plus only" (beats.4.vo): the feature limits say early accounts have different entitlements, so "only" overstates exclusivity.
Category view showing the note listed there (beats.3 shot): no source evidence for this view in the cited feature.
